title: The Kinsman-Redeemer
lead: The go'el was the near relative who stepped in to rescue a family member: buying back sold land or a relative sold into slavery, and avenging a murder. In Ruth the redeemer also takes on a widow's marriage, a link scholars still debate. The prophets and psalms call God Israel's Redeemer, and the New Testament speaks of redemption through Christ.

sections.h: The redeemer in the Law and the Prophets
sections.b: The Law names three tasks for the go'el: buying back family land that has been sold (Leviticus 25:25–34), buying back a relative who has sold himself into slavery (Leviticus 25:47–55), and avenging a murdered relative as "the avenger of blood" (Numbers 35:9–28). Jeremiah buys his cousin's field as a redeemer, as a sign of hope during the Babylonian siege (Jeremiah 32:6–15). God takes the title for himself, especially in Isaiah 40–66, about ten times in chapters 40–55: "I am the LORD your God... your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 43:3, 14), and Job cries, "I know that my redeemer lives" (Job 19:25).
